Transcript Body:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey Emily, thanks for taking time, um, really quick intro, I'm Alex, recruiting at Redwood. Jordan is our... our infra hiring manager. uh, how's it going?
[00:08] Emily Chen: Hey Alex, thanks — excited to chat. Doing well.
[00:10] Jordan Patel: Hi Emily, nice to meet you. real quick, can you walk us through your current role at Aurora and what you do day-to-day?
[00:18] Emily Chen: Sure. I'm a staff ML engineer on the recommendations platform. Mostly I own model serving and productionization for ranking models — so inference pipelines, model packaging with ONNX and sometimes TensorRT, autoscaling on k8s, and cost optimizations. I also worked on a small team that built a prefix cache for cold-starts, and we maintain some private deployments for a couple large clients.
[00:37] Jordan Patel: Nice. When you say prefix cache — can you expand? was it in-memory? redis? KV cash?
[00:42] Emily Chen: Yeah sorry, K V cache, it's a mix. We used Redis for short-term prefix caches and a local in-process LM cache for hot prefixes to minimize round trips. For larger state we persisted to a regional memcached cluster. It was lightweight, mostly to avoid re-embedding common user sequences.
[00:58] Alex Kim: (laughs) there we go, the classic K V cash vs KV cache transcription.
[01:02] Jordan Patel: How did you reason about invalidation and freshness? that's often where caches go wrong in recommender land.
[01:07] Emily Chen: We had a TTL plus event-based invalidation — when a user had a major event, e.g., purchase, we invalidated key prefixes. It wasn't perfect, and we accepted eventual consistency. Latency SLO for 95th pctl was 120ms for the endpoint, so caching gave us the p95 headroom.
[01:25] Jordan Patel: Good. Did you do any quantization or kernel-level tuning to reduce latency/cost?
[01:29] Emily Chen: Yep. For smaller models we would quantize to int8 with ONNX quantization. For the bigger ranking model we tried 4-bit QAT but at the time the accuracy drop was surprising, so we hybridized — weight-only quant on some layers. We also used TRT for lower-latency GPU paths and fusing ops.
[01:47] Alex Kim: How hands-on were you with the infra for Triton/TensorRT or was that an ops team?
[01:52] Emily Chen: I set up the model servers and optimized the inference workflows — so I wrote the Docker images, CI that produced ONNX artifacts, and tuned TensorRT profiles. The SRE team helped with fleet autoscaling but I owned the micro-benchmarks and the kernel selection experiments.
[02:05] Jordan Patel: Cool. At Redwood we do a lot of routing decisions — some customers pin to hosted models, some need private VPCs. Do you have experience with private deployments or VPC networking for inference?
[02:16] Emily Chen: Yes, we had a couple customers on dedicated clusters behind private peering. I handled cert rotation and KMS integrations for model artifact encryption. Also wrote some of the deployment manifests for air-gapped installs — though the ops team did the actual on-prem install.
[02:31] Jordan Patel: Any compliance or SOC2-related work?
[02:33] Emily Chen: I helped with audit logs for model access and added fields to our access events, and we integrated with company KMS for at-rest model encryption. I didn't run the audit but supported queries for the compliance team.
[02:44] Alex Kim: Nice, that's relevant. Quick recruiter Q: what are you looking for next — IC vs people manager, relocation, compensation, timeline?
[02:51] Emily Chen: I'm looking for staff-level IC role. Remote is fine but prefer US timezone overlap. Timeline, I'm interviewing now — early-stage offers coming in, hoping to decide in 4–6 weeks. Compensation is flexible but target around mid-to-senior staff band.
[03:06] Jordan Patel: Good to know. On the technical side — can you sketch a high-level design for how you'd serve a large LLM for a low-latency product that needs <100ms p50 and 300ms p95 for a 512 token output?
[03:18] Emily Chen: Sure. I'd look at a few levers: model size vs latency — prefer a distilled model or a smaller encoder-decoder variant for that SLO. Horizontal sharding helps: maintain many warm GPU actors with KV cache for prefix states so you reduce sequential decoding stalls. Use batching up to a latency budget with dynamic batching tuned per-traffic pattern. For kernel/compilation, precompile optimized kernels for our typical sequence lengths and use int8 or 4-bit when it preserves quality. Also have a fallback to CPU or a smaller model on overload.
[03:50] Jordan Patel: Can you explain the warm actor concept?
[03:52] Emily Chen: Yeah, warm actors are long-lived model processes that keep KV cache and loaded weights resident, so subsequent requests that hit the same actor avoid load/unload overhead. We pinned actors to GPUs and used soft-affinity routing by user shard to improve cache locality.
[04:05] Alex Kim: There's often confusion about routing and locality — how did you protect against stragglers and hot keys?
[04:10] Emily Chen: We had load-shedding policies and request queue depth limits; for hot keys we replicated state across a small number of actors and used an LRU for less-traveled prefixes. For serious hot keys we used request-level throttles and rate-limited the upstream event generator.
[04:25] Jordan Patel: Sounds practical. Do you have experience with cost attribution or per-route cost analytics?
[04:29] Emily Chen: We had a simple token-cost model where we estimated GPU time and tracked token usage per route; that informed batching and caching decisions. I wrote gauges to break down p50/p95 latency and cost per template.
[04:39] Jordan Patel: Awesome. Any hands-on with model rollouts and canarying?
[04:42] Emily Chen: Yes, we did traffic splits with weighted rollouts and automated rollback on regression. We had eval hooks that ran on a small percentage of traffic to compare outputs and trigger alerts.
[04:52] Alex Kim: Switching gears, what's an interview question you found most challenging recently?
[04:56] Emily Chen: There was a systems design problem on multi-tenant GPU scheduling — balancing fairness and tail latency. I proposed a priority queue plus token-bucket scheduler with preemption of low-priority batch jobs.
[05:07] Jordan Patel: Nice. For this role, you'd be working closely with infra and product. How comfortable are you writing production infra vs model code?
[05:15] Emily Chen: Comfortable doing both. My day-to-day is often infra-adjacent, CI, deployment, benchmarks, and then model performance tweaks. I enjoy the full stack.
[05:22] Jordan Patel: Quick question about telemetry — how did you track quality regressions after quantization?
[05:27] Emily Chen: We used A/B with holdout prompts and a few human-eval metrics plus automated unit tests for token-level perplexity and some business KPIs. If quant caused drift beyond threshold, we prevented rollout.
[05:38] Alex Kim: Candidate question time — any questions for us about the team or role?
[05:42] Emily Chen: Yeah — curious how the infra team is split between hosted and private customers? And what's the on-call expectation?
[05:49] Jordan Patel: We have two infra pods — one focused on the hosted control plane and another on private/dedicated customers; engineers often cross-collaborate. On-call is shared, roughly 1:8 rotation with pager for Sev1. We aim to keep infra tooling to limit page noise.
[06:02] Emily Chen: Sounds reasonable. Another practical question — do you expect engineers to own customer-facing installs for private deployments?
[06:09] Jordan Patel: For the private team, yes, engineers may assist with triage and runbooks for installs, but we have a delivery ops team that does most of the heavy lifting; infra engineers interface and own technical designs.
[06:19] Emily Chen: Great. One more — what's the interview loop look like?
[06:22] Alex Kim: Typically it's a take-home assignment, then a technical loop with infra + product + a coding/cs deep dive. For staff roles we add a system design and leadership interview.
[06:31] Emily Chen: Ok that aligns. I'm comfortable with a take-home.
[06:34] Jordan Patel: Any red flags we should know about? or constraints like visa status?
[06:38] Emily Chen: I'm a US citizen, nothing blocking.
[06:41] Alex Kim: Great. A few behavioral things — can you give an example of when you pushed back on a tradeoff?
[06:46] Emily Chen: At Aurora we had a customer requesting extremely aggressive SLOs; the product owner wanted to add model checkpoints to meet accuracy but that increased latency. I pushed for a hybrid approach: live model for critical decisions and an async re-ranker to reconcile results. It reduced latency impact and addressed accuracy concerns.
[07:07] Jordan Patel: That shows pragmatism. Follow-up on quant — did you ever implement QAT?
[07:11] Emily Chen: We tried QAT for a medium sized model; it reduced float32 drop but training cost increased and CI got heavier. We kept it for a couple models where accuracy matters, but most production cases used post-training quant with careful calibration.
[07:24] Alex Kim: Ok, one final ops-y question — have you scaled auto-batching? any libraries or custom?
[07:30] Emily Chen: We used a mix. For PyTorch serving we used TorchServe's batching for a bit then moved to a custom async batching layer that allowed priority preemption and batch compaction.
[07:40] Jordan Patel: Did you run into head-of-line blocking?
[07:42] Emily Chen: Yes — we added prioritized lanes and time windows to ensure small latency-critical requests didn't wait behind large batches.
[07:49] Alex Kim: Good. Closing — any other questions for us?
[07:52] Emily Chen: Not right now. I'll wait for the take-home.
[07:55] Jordan Patel: We'll review and get the take-home out. Alex will follow up with role specifics and comp band.
[08:02] Alex Kim: Cool. Thanks Emily, appreciate the time. We'll follow up by Tuesday with the assignment.
[08:07] Emily Chen: Thanks, talk soon.
[08:09] (call ends — note: timestamps in the transcript are approximate; the call ended at 15:32 PST)

Notes on transcription quality: some terms like "KV cache" transcribed as "K V cash" in auto notes; proper nouns (Triton/ TensorRT) occasionally garbled.
